newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU backs plan to defuse Helms-Burton row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU backs plan to defuse Helms-Burton row.

text.p: European Union ambassadors backed a plan on Wednesday to defuse a row with Washington over U.S. anti-Cuba legislation, but set a Friday deadline for formal endorsement by national capitals, EU diplomats said.
"There is an agreement," a diplomat said.
Full details of the accord, which will be adopted on Friday unless any EU state objects, were not immediately available.
A second diplomat complained of European Commission tactics in securing a stand-off with Washington on Cuba policy and then presenting member states with a done deal.
"The Commission presented member states with a fait accompli," said the diplomat, who added that endorsement in national capitals was by no means automatic.
Another said the EU accord would include a clause to automatically restart the bloc's World Trade Organisation complaint if talks with Washington break down.
It would also condemn the "extra-territorial" effects of the U.S. law, the diplomat added.

France, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Belgium were said earlier to have been insistent that endorsement be accompanied by the threat to reopen the WTO disputes panel if Washington took any action against EU companies.
Ambassadors agreed on Monday to postpone the WTO complaint but left until Wednesday their considered reaction.
The Commission and Washington agreed on Friday to negotiate a compromise in policy towards Cuba, which the United States has targeted with its Helms-Burton legislation.

They would also work toward a global agreement on protection of expropriated property. The White House would in exchange seek to change a key provision of Helms-Burton barring executives of companies that invest in disputed properties in Cuba from entering the United States.

The Helms-Burton legislation, an amalgam of U.S. anti-Cuba laws, has outraged Washington's trading partners by threatening various punishments against foreign firms doing certain kinds of business in Cuba.

The row and its resulting WTO panel have strained transatlantic relations and put the WTO disputes procedures to a test that many leading trading countries would like to avoid so early in the organisation's existence.
EU officials said the sensitivity of the issue had been underlined by France, which urged the ambassadors not to talk to journalists about the issue until a decision had been made.
